cards.explanation: The enemies' plan flipped, friends: on the thirteenth of Adar, the Jews overpowered those who hated them. The text says the enemies had hoped to overpower the Jews, but “…their plan was overturned and the Jews overpowered those who hated them.” (Esther 9:1) You ever plan your whole day down to the minute, and the day shows up with its own ideas? Same energy, except this was a much bigger deal.

The answer is False. The text says, “No man could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples.” (Esther 9:2) That's the thirteenth of Adar, friends. Not one man could stand against them. Not ONE!

The reason is that the fear of them had fallen on all peoples. The verse gives it itself: “…because the fear of them had fallen upon all peoples.” (Esther 9:2) That's the only reason it gives, so I'll stop there. Sometimes the best thing a verse does is just tell you.

The officials and the rest of the provincial leaders helped the Jews. The text lists them all: the officials, the satraps, the governors, and the king's administrators, and says they “…helped the Jews…” (Esther 9:3). That's a whole government lineup on one side, friends. I've never had that many folks helping with one batch, and I once had a very good week.

The name is Mordecai, Queen Esther's cousin (Esther 2:7). The verse says the officials helped “…because the fear of Mordecai had fallen upon them.” (Esther 9:3) The next verse adds that he exercised great power in the palace and his fame spread through the provinces (Esther 9:4). A name that travels that far, I can only dream about. My name spread as far as the end of one counter.

The number is five hundred. The text says, “In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men…” (Esther 9:6). I think this is one of the heavier numbers in the story, friends, so let's just let it be a heavy number. It's the count the king hears about later (Esther 9:12).

The answer is True, and it's worth noticing. The text says the Jews killed Haman's ten sons, “…but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:10) Haman, son of Hammedatha, was the man who had plotted against the Jews (Esther 3:6). The king's letter had allowed plunder (Esther 8:11), and the text says they didn't take it.

King Xerxes wants to know what Queen Esther's petition is. He says, “Now what is your petition? It will be given to you.” (Esther 9:12) He asked her the same sort of thing before (Esther 5:6; 7:2). I like a king who keeps the door open, friends. I spent years stuck in a junk drawer that never did.
The answer is tomorrow. Esther says, “…may the Jews in Susa also have tomorrow to carry out today’s edict…” (Esther 9:13). She asks for one more day, friends, nothing longer.

The answer is False. King Xerxes does not turn Esther down. The text says, “So the king commanded that this be done.” (Esther 9:14) An edict was issued in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman. He had said her requests would be fulfilled (Esther 9:12), and that's what happened.

The number is three hundred. On the fourteenth of Adar, the Jews in Susa came together again and “…put to death three hundred men there…” (Esther 9:15). I'll leave it just as the text gives it, friends. The verse also says they didn't lay a hand on the plunder.

The number is 75,000. The text says, “They killed 75,000 who hated them, but they did not lay a hand on the plunder.” (Esther 9:16) That's the count the text gives for the royal provinces, and I'll let it stand. And again, friends, the plunder stays untouched.

The answer is True! The verse says, “…on the fourteenth day they rested, making it a day of feasting and joy.” (Esther 9:17) After a heavy stretch, the day ends in rest, friends. I'll take a day of rest and feasting any time, as long as nobody asks me to clean the oven.

The answer is the fifteenth. The Jews in Susa assembled on the thirteenth and the fourteenth, “So they rested on the fifteenth day, making it a day of feasting and joy.” (Esther 9:18) They got their rest one day later than the Jews in the provinces did. Same joy, friends, different day on the calendar.

The village Jews send gifts to one another. The verse calls the fourteenth of Adar “…a holiday for sending gifts to one another.” (Esther 9:19) I'm a big fan of any holiday where gifts go around, friends. Nobody in that line is left holding an empty box.
